meta.title: Haneul Park (하늘공원) | Seoul's Ecological Park in Mapo-gu · Silver-grass Meadow & Sunset
meta.description: The complete guide to Haneul Park (하늘공원): an ecological oasis in Seoul's Mapo-gu, transformed from a former landfill within World Cup Park. Silver-grass meadows, Han River sunsets and the Seoul skyline — all in one place. Opening hours, how to get there, the accessible shuttle, visitor reviews and photo spots.

nonprofitBanner.text: This is an independent, non-profit guide compiled by travel enthusiasts to provide the most objective information about visiting Haneul Park. It is free, and we are affiliated with no organization.

mission.title: Our Mission
mission.text: So that every traveler who visits Seoul does not miss this oasis reborn from a garbage mountain inside World Cup Park, we have gathered scattered official information into this guide — purely to give you the most authentic viewing and cultural experience.

hero.title: Haneul Park (하늘공원)
hero.subtitle: An ecological oasis in Seoul's Mapo-gu, inside World Cup Park — reborn from a former landfill. Free to enter, it is Seoul's top spot for silver-grass meadows, Han River sunsets and the city skyline. Climb the eco-hill and watch the afterglow spread across the skyline.

hiddenRules.title: Safety Tips for the Hill & Slopes
hiddenRules.subtitle: Haneul Park sits on an ~90 m ecological hill; the ascent stairs (the famous 'Haneul Park stairs') are steep. Know these in advance for a safe, smooth climb.

highlights.label: Stairs & gradient
highlights.note: About 291 ecological stairs from Peace Park to the summit — physically demanding. Wear comfy shoes, slow down and rest in stages.

highlights.label: Sun & wind
highlights.note: The hill is open with little shade; sunscreen and water in summer, warm layers for the strong river wind in autumn/winter. Light fades after sunset — plan ahead.

highlights.label: Night & descent
highlights.note: Some slopes have limited lighting before closing; descents stress the knees — elders and children should use the gentle loop or the eco-shuttle.

panels.q: Do I have to climb the stairs? Is there an alternative?
panels.a: The classic route is about 291 ecological stairs and fairly steep. Those with limited stamina, infants or reduced mobility can take the park's eco-shuttle (eco-shuttle) along the service road straight to the upper platform, avoiding the climb.
items: The shuttle has fixed stops and a fare; queues form in peak season — go off-peak.
Strollers and wheelchairs can reach the summit platform via the upper road.

panels.a: The park closes around sunset; light drops quickly afterwards and some slopes are dimly lit, plus the descent is hard on the knees. Start going down right after sunset, or take the last shuttle.

panels.q: Can I picnic, light a fire or fly a drone on the grass?
panels.a: The silver-grass slope is a protected zone — no stepping on, sitting on or picking the grass. The area is windy and near flight paths, so drones are prohibited without permission. Use the designated paths and take your trash with you.

complianceGuide.title: Haneul Park · Visitor & Ecological Etiquette
complianceGuide.subtitle: This is both a citizen's green space and a habitat we must protect together. Following these rules is basic respect for nature and others.

rules.title: No entering or picking the grass
rules.text: The silver-grass slope is a protected ecological zone — do not step on, sit on or pick the grass; stay on the paved paths and boardwalks.
items: Stop immediately at signs reading 'Protect the turf' or 'No entry'.
For photos, never step onto the slope or trample vegetation for a better angle.

rules.title: Take your trash with you
rules.text: Bins at the top and on the slope are limited and the wind scatters litter. Bring a small bag and take everything away when you leave.

rules.title: Quiet viewing
rules.text: Many come specifically to watch the sunset and city nightscape in silence. Before and around sunset, please lower your voice and avoid loud music.

rules.title: No smoking or open flame
rules.text: The grass is highly flammable in dry seasons — the whole park is smoke-free; no open flame, BBQ or smoking, to prevent fire.

intro.title: Getting to Know Haneul Park
intro.description: Haneul Park (하늘공원, Haneul Park) sits inside World Cup Park in Seoul's Mapo-gu — an ecological park built atop the former Nanjido (난지도) landfill. '하늘' means 'sky' in Korean, and the park takes its name from the high hill that seems to touch the sky. It is both Seoul citizens' weekend green lung for climbing, reed-viewing and sunsets, and a symbol of 'waste-to-wonder' environmental regeneration — once Seoul's largest garbage mountain, now an ecological oasis where silver-grass sways and migratory birds rest.

visitGuide.title: Visitor Guide
visitGuide.description: Haneul Park is free and open daily, roughly 06:00–22:00 (seasonal). Make a dusk summit for the sunset your main plan, then link Peace Park, Nanji Hangang Park and the World Cup Stadium. The summit is open with minimal facilities — do your supplies at the foot (Peace Park) or nearby commercial areas.
items: Free and open daily; dusk summit for sunset and skyline is best for light and photos.
Best angles are the southwest slope and viewing deck; autumn silver-grass (eulalia) is most spectacular.
From Line 6 World Cup Stadium Stn (월드컵경기장) Exit 1, walk ~15 min to the foot, then climb the stairs or take the shuttle.
No shops or food at the top; water and restrooms are at the foot (Peace Park) and Nanjicheon — stock up beforehand.

transportSection.overviewText: Haneul Park is inside World Cup Park in Seoul's Mapo-gu. The easiest external link is flying into Incheon (ICN)/Gimpo (GMP) or taking the KTX to Seoul Station, then the subway. In the city, the park is next to Line 6 World Cup Stadium Stn (월드컵경기장); transferring from Line 2/AREX usually takes ~30–50 min. Haneul Park is an ~90 m eco-hill — from the foot you climb 291 stairs or take the eco-shuttle.
transportSection.overviewText2: The park is an open ecological area with no walls or gates. Plan transport, parking and the summit route together — the shuttle greatly reduces the climb, especially with elders, infants or luggage.

No large dedicated lot at the summit — use World Cup Park's public parking or nearby paid lots, then walk/shuttle up.
During the autumn reed festival and weekends crowds are heavy; parking and stairs jam — strongly prefer transit or off-peak.

officialManagement.title: About the Park
officialManagement.text: Haneul Park is an ecological park in Seoul's Mapo-gu, inside World Cup Park, transformed from the former Nanjido landfill and managed by the Seoul Metropolitan Government as urban green space. Long a public place for citizens to climb, view reeds and watch the sunset, it is also a symbol of 'resource cycling' and 'environmental regeneration' for the city.

humanities.title: History & Transformation
humanities.subtitle: Following the landfill closure, ecological regeneration and on-site signs, we present the history of Haneul Park — from garbage mountain to urban oasis.

sections.title: From garbage mountain to Haneul Park
sections.content: Nanjido (난지도), where Haneul Park stands, was Seoul's largest landfill from 1978 to 1993, receiving most of the city's household waste in mounds tens of meters high. After closure, the city stabilized the hill with thick soil cover and grass, and leveraged the 2002 Korea-Japan World Cup to promote environmental regeneration — opening in 1999 as part of 'World Cup Park' under the name 'Haneul Park'. '하늘 (sky)' refers both to its towering height and to the city's upward transformation.

sections.title: Closure & ecological regeneration
sections.content: After closure, soil and vegetation gradually stabilized the hill, and pioneer plants such as silver-grass (eulalia) naturally colonized it into a unique upland meadow. Today it is not only a rare urban meadow in Seoul but also a stopover for migratory birds and a window for stargazing and sunset — the once foul-smelling garbage mountain has become the city's 'green lung'.

sections.title: Part of World Cup Park
sections.content: Haneul Park forms 'World Cup Park' together with Peace Park, Pyeonghwa (Peace) Park, Nakji (Orchid) Park, Noeul (Sunset) Park and Haneul (Sky) Park — a representative environmental regeneration landmark of Seoul. It weaves 'waste treatment — ecological restoration — public recreation' into a readable urban narrative.

sections.title: Stairs & ecological design
sections.content: The park reaches the summit via the famous 291 ecological stairs, preserving the ritual of climbing while also serving elders, children and the less mobile — an upper service road carries the eco-shuttle (eco-shuttle). The grass is ringed by boardwalks to minimize trampling, a model of 'low-impact development'.

sections.title: Citizens' sky living room
sections.content: Today Haneul Park has shifted from a barren hill to an urban green space anyone can reach. Free and open, it draws morning exercisers and dusk sunset-watchers, and during the autumn reed festival becomes a citywide event — a node where Seoul's daily life and tourism meet.

sections.title: A symbol of Seoul's regeneration
sections.content: From garbage mountain to oasis, Haneul Park is seen as a spiritual corner of Seoul's urban transformation and sustainable development, echoing the global 'waste-to-wonder' narrative. It reminds us that great urban landmarks often come from a gentler treatment of the land.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: Nanjido, where Haneul Park stands, received most of Seoul's household waste from 1978 to 1993, with mounds tens of meters high. Today, covered in soil and greenery, the autumn silver-grass ripples in the wind — few would guess a garbage mountain lies beneath their feet.

sitePlaques.title: Reading the On-site Signs
sitePlaques.subtitle: When you visit, official signs and maps at the foot and summit are the most authoritative first-hand source on its regeneration history. We translate and explain each one.
sitePlaques.intro: The following readings are based on on-site photos of the Seoul Metropolitan Government's regeneration signs, ecological maps and shuttle instructions.

items.title: Nanjido landfill & World Cup Park regeneration
items.koTitleZh: Nanjido Landfill & World Cup Park Development
items.body: The sign records: Nanjido was Seoul's largest household-waste landfill (1978–1993); after closure it was ecologically restored with soil cover and greenery, and World Cup Park was built for the 2002 Korea-Japan World Cup. Haneul Park opened in 1999 as part of it — a public green space for citizens to climb and view the river.

items.title: Silver-grass, birds & meadow ecology
items.body: The bilingual eco sign explains: the Haneul Park meadow naturally succeeded after landfill soil cover, with silver-grass (eulalia) as the dominant pioneer plant; in autumn the reeds turn snow-white, and in spring/summer it hosts insects and migratory birds — reminding visitors not to enter the slope and to protect it together.

items.title: Stairs, boardwalk & eco-shuttle
items.body: The park map marks: 291 ecological stairs to the summit; an upper road for the eco-shuttle (eco-shuttle) with fixed stops and a fare; the grass ringed by boardwalks, with wheelchairs and strollers reaching the summit platform via the upper road. Note last-departure times and suspension in bad weather.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Practical info about Haneul Park's facilities, history and visit planning.

items.label: Parking
items.value: World Cup Park combined / foot lot

items.q: Is there parking, and what are the rates?
items.a: No large dedicated lot at the summit, but World Cup Park combined parking (Peace Park underground/surface, public rates) and the foot temporary lot are reachable, then walk or take the eco-shuttle. Rates vary by season; they fill fast on weekends/peak, so arrive early or prefer transit.

items.q: Are wheelchairs or strollers allowed in the area?
items.a: The summit platform and upper road are reachable by the eco-shuttle (eco-shuttle), so wheelchairs and strollers can reach the upper viewing area; but the classic 291 stairs are steep with no ramp — the lower-to-upper move needs the shuttle. The boardwalks are gentle and good for pushing.

items.q: Are there restrooms or food at the site?
items.a: The summit slope has no shops or food; the nearest water and public toilets are at the foot (Peace Park), Nanjicheon and the combined parking (~10–15 min walk back). Stock up before going up.

items.q: Why is it called 'Haneul (Sky)', and does it relate to the garbage mountain?
items.a: '하늘' means sky; the park sits on an ~90 m eco-hill that seems to touch the sky, hence 'Haneul Park'. Its predecessor was Seoul's largest Nanjido landfill — the name and the land together tell a regeneration story from garbage mountain to oasis.

items.q: What is special about its ecology and landform?
items.a: After landfill closure and soil cover, pioneer plants like silver-grass naturally formed a meadow — now a stopover for migratory birds and a window for stargazing and sunset; the stairs-plus-shuttle design is also a model of 'low-impact development' and sustainability.
Haneul Park is a public ecological park, free daily ~06:00–22:00 (seasonal), with no gate, no ticket and no reservation — visit anytime.

items.q: How long does a visit take?
items.a: A typical summit takes about 1–2 hours (stairs/shuttle plus time at the top); allow half a day if adding Peace Park, Nanji Hangang Park and the World Cup Stadium.

items.q: Can I still go in bad weather?
items.a: Yes — it is an open park, visitable in any weather. But the summit slope is windy; in thunderstorms or snow it gets slippery with low visibility — wear grippy shoes, watch the weather and closing time; the eco-shuttle may suspend in bad weather.

items.q: After visiting, what other attractions are worth it?
items.a: From Haneul Park you can link Peace Park, Nakji (Orchid) Park, Nanji Hangang Park (wetlands & cycling), the Seoul World Cup Stadium, and farther out Hongdae/Mangwon Market and Yeouido Hangang Park — a half-day 'eco–culture–food' line in western Seoul.

education.title: Why did a garbage mountain become Haneul Park? (Meaning of Regeneration)
education.subtitle: A small hill built on garbage — why did it cross eras to become Seoul's environmental symbol? Behind it are layered narratives of waste, land and city memory.

points.title: Origin of waste and land
points.text: Nanjido received most of Seoul's household waste, mounds tens of meters high; after closure the city reborn the land most gently, and Haneul Park is the start of that restoration.

points.title: Citizens' sky corridor
points.text: As part of World Cup Park, it shifted from barren hill to an urban green space anyone can reach, carrying Seoul citizens' daily life of climbing, river-viewing and rest.

points.title: A link of memory
points.text: The same hill connects landfill history, meadow ecology, and today's sunset and skyline. It reminds us: great urban landmarks are often where history and reality coexist.

audience.title: Who Finds Resonance Here? (Audience Guide)
audience.subtitle: Different visitors each find their best 'way in'.

items.resonance: Free, open and safe urban green space; kids can see reeds, view the Han River and easily summit by eco-shuttle.
items.tip: Take the shuttle up; combine Peace Park lawn and Nanji Hangang cycling — adjust order by stamina.

items.resonance: Dusk sunset and city nightscape are Seoul's most romantic frames, with high shot rates.
items.tip: Secure the summit deck 60–90 min before sunset; shoot blue moment for both lights and sky color.

items.resonance: As a meadow sample reborn from a landfill, the silver-grass succession and migratory birds are worth a close look.
items.tip: Link Haneul Park with Nanji Hangang wetlands into an 'urban ecology tour'.

items.resonance: No need to go far — observe reed meadows and Han River sunsets right in Seoul; also link subway, the World Cup Stadium and local food — the ideal start to understand Seoul's urban transformation.
items.tip: Take Line 6 to World Cup Stadium Stn, then walk/shuttle.

lodging.title: Stay Guide: Near the Park, or Convenient?
lodging.subtitle: Seoul is a city 'where river meets city'. We do not recommend specific hotels, but help you read two lodging patterns to choose what fits you.

options.name: Hongdae / Hapjeong (Mapo core)
options.highlight: Stay in Hongdae or Hapjeong and Line 6 and AREX are at your door, making Haneul Park, the World Cup Stadium and Yeouido easy; the night street food and craft markets suit young travelers. Best for those focused on 'city roam + eco park' with high convenience.
points: To Haneul Park by subway ~15–30 min, one transfer.
Dining, shopping and nightlife extremely rich.
More choices, usually better value.

options.name: Mapo / Yeouido riverside
options.highlight: Stay along the Han in Mapo or Yeouido; morning riverside walks and cycling, then subway to Haneul Park. Best for those focused on 'river, sunset, slow family trips'.
points: Han River Park and bike paths at your door, good for mornings and families.
Quieter than Hongdae, good for rest.
To Haneul Park by subway ~20–30 min.

lodging.peak: In Seoul's spring/autumn peak (especially the October reed festival and April cherry season) and holidays, rooms tighten as tourists flood in and prices rise clearly. Book weeks ahead; if booking near a holiday, widen the search to Jongno, Gangnam and other areas, then take the subway back.
tips: For sunset: prefer Mapo/Yeouido riverside, river views morning and dusk.
For convenience and nightlife: choose Hongdae/Hapjeong, transit and dining at hand.
Before booking, confirm breakfast, parking and EV chargers (key for drivers).
In peak season and holidays plan ahead to avoid no-room or high prices.
